extractedText: MILWAUKEE BREWERSMilwaukee BrewersAdd TopicHenderson, Patrick combine for dominant outing in Brewers' win over Twins Curt HoggMilwaukee Journal SentinelUpdated May 16, 2026, 11:50 p.m. ETHear this storyMINNEAPOLIS – Chad Patrick, he himself will tell you, can be a textbook overthinker. Bullpen Chad, though? That’s a different story. Remove the nervous anticipation, the ruminating, the stomach-churning, and replace it instead with cutters. Lots and lots of cutters.“It’s kind of an indescribable feeling,” Patrick said of pitching out of the bullpen. “That’s where the thought process comes into it. Not worrying, like when I’m starting, about how deep I’m going to go in the game. Whereas I come in from the bullpen and I don’t know how many outs I’m in for.” On May 16 at Target Field, it turned out to be 12 outs as Patrick along with starter Logan Henderson joined forces and stymied the Minnesota Twins’ bats for all nine innings, making Jackson Chourio’s sixth-inning home run hold up in a 2-1 win for the Milwaukee Brewers. Those two guys, to throw nine innings and keep them to one run is fantastic,” said Brewers manager Pat Murphy. Patrick, it’s clear after three relief outings over the past eight days, is in the role that best fits him, at least for the time being. Henderson is, too – and his comes sans caveat.A year ago, Henderson wasn’t able to get solid footing in the big-league rotation despite doing all he could to firmly plant himself in the footholds. Henderson, in five outings, displayed a remarkable ability to deliver quality each time he was called upon, yet was deployed as a spot starter with no room in the rotation. Even this spring, the 24-year-old began this year in Class AAA Nashville.Patrick was one of the arms keeping Henderson out of The Good Land and stationed on Broadway. Patrick opened the season in the Brewers’ rotation, a spot he earned as a rookie in 2025, before shakiness across his first seven outings gave Milwaukee’s decision-makers a different idea: Move him to the bullpen. Patrick and Henderson are now where they’re meant to be, and in Minnesota, teamed up to make one big pitch after another to fuel the Brewers to a fifth straight series win.Henderson pitched five innings as the starter, allowing a solo homer to Trevor Larnach but nothing more while fanning seven, and Patrick took care of everything else with four dominant innings in relief in which he only allowed one Twin to reach.The right-handers found themselves in one highly precarious spot apiece, but worked out without any damage, holding the Twins 0 for 10 with runners in scoring position. Henderson faced a tense situation in the second, when he put together a crash course on gritting through an inning.It began with a Josh Bell lob wedge on a pitch at his ankles for a leadoff single, then he moved to third when Kody Clemens pulled a low stinger down the line in right for a double when Henderson left one too far up in the zone.Henderson didn't have great feel or confidence with his changeup, his bread and butter, even stepping off in a 3-2 count against Tristan Gray because he was only comfortable with his fastball. Gray drew a walk to load the bases with one out.Then, Henderson buckled down. After seven straight fastballs, he went back to the change to strike out James Outman, then put Austin Martin away by mixing speeds and finishing him off with a cutter down.“There’s not time to make adjustments after a few batters,” Henderson said of the jam. “Make it after each pitch. That was the mindset.” When Henderson handed the ball off to Patrick, it marked his ninth consecutive start to begin his career with no more than two runs allowed.“I didn’t feel like I had my best stuff in that [second] inning leading,” Henderson said. “I felt the changeup was a lot better late in the game. Honestly, the first three innings I didn’t feel like I executed many pitches at all. Kind of found it the last two innings. Made a little mechanical and mindset adjustment and was able to find it.” Patrick got some assistance during his jam from Chourio, whose solo homer on the first pitch of the sixth against Twins left-hander Connor Prielipp – a Tomah native who grew up rooting for the Brewers – gave Milwaukee a 2-1 lead. With the tying run on third and one out after James Outman tripled, the left fielder ranged from deep left to make a sliding grab for the second out. Helping the matter for the Brewers was Outman’s decision to not tag up even though Chourio was in a difficult position to come up throwing after his long feet-first slide. “Off the bat, I saw it was shallow there, so I knew I was going to have to get after it a little bit,” Chourio said. “That’s what I did.
